1.title: Generative AI: Core Concepts
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Generative A I, Core Concepts. This module opens Domain two and covers task statement two point one. You will learn what foundation models and large language models are, what tokens, chunks, embeddings and vectors mean, how generative A I is used and priced, and the first ideas behind agents: tools, memory, multi-agent patterns and the Model Context Protocol.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Define tokens, chunking, embeddings, vectors, transformers, L L Ms, foundation models, multi-modal models and diffusion models. Name use cases for generative A I. Describe the foundation model lifecycle. Explain token-based pricing and context engineering. And define agentic A I ideas: multi-agent patterns, M C P, memory, tools and orchestration.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Starts a GenAI Pilot
1.text: Cedar and Salt Travel picks two pilots: summaries of long guest reviews, and a booking assistant. The engineers use words the leaders do not know: tokens, embeddings, chunks and agents. Finance asks two questions: what will this cost, and why does a longer answer cost more? Your job is to explain the core ideas in plain words.

1.title: Foundation Models and Large Language Models
1.text: A foundation model, or F M, is a very large deep learning model trained on broad, unlabeled data. It learns by self-supervised learning, which means it makes its own labels from the data. One F M handles many tasks, steered by prompts, instead of needing one model per task. A large language model, or L L M, is a foundation model for language: text in, text out. Developers build on an existing F M instead of training from scratch. Exam tip: many tasks from one model, steered by a prompt, means a foundation model.

1.title: Transformers and Multi-Modal Models
1.text: A transformer is a neural network with self-attention that reads a whole sequence at once. Most L L Ms are transformer-based, and they can have billions of parameters. A multi-modal model works with more than one kind of data: text, images, audio or video. For example, it can describe a photo, or answer a question about a chart. Other F M designs exist too, such as diffusion models for images. Exam tip: text, images and audio together mean multi-modal, and a transformer uses self-attention over a sequence.

1.title: Diffusion Models
1.text: A diffusion model generates images, and video, from noise. In training, noise is added to an image step by step until only noise is left. The model then learns to reverse it: it removes the noise step by step to get a clear image. Typical uses are text-to-image, image-to-image, editing and video creation. A text prompt steers what the image shows. Exam tip: images from noise, removed step by step, mean a diffusion model.

1.title: Tokens
1.text: A token is a small unit of text the model reads and writes: a word, part of a word, or punctuation. The model predicts the next token, one at a time. Every model has a context window, which is the most tokens it can handle at once, input plus output. Longer prompts and answers use more tokens, which means more cost and more time. Images and audio are also turned into tokens or similar units. Exam tip: tokens are the unit of length, of limits and of billing.

1.title: Embeddings and Vectors
1.text: An embedding is a numerical representation of an item, such as a piece of text, that captures its meaning. The numbers form a vector, which is a list of values in a multi-dimensional space. Items with similar meaning have vectors that are close together. That lets software find things by meaning, not only by exact words. Uses include semantic search, recommendations and retrieval for generative A I. Exam tip: an embedding is meaning as numbers, a vector is the list of numbers, and close vectors mean similar meaning.

1.title: Chunking and Vector Search
1.text: Here is how documents become searchable by meaning. The figure shows five steps. Chunking splits long documents into smaller pieces that fit the model and keep one idea each. Each chunk becomes an embedding, stored in a vector index. A question is embedded too, and the closest chunks are returned. Chunking strategies include fixed-size chunks, hierarchical parent and child chunks, and semantic chunks. Exam tip: chunk, embed, store, then search by closeness of meaning.

1.title: Prompt Engineering in One Slide
1.text: A prompt is the input you give a model: an instruction, plus any context or examples. Prompt engineering is crafting prompts to get better answers. No retraining is needed; you just change the words. Prompts can set a role, a format and limits. Module eight covers techniques such as zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought. Exam tip: changing the prompt is the cheapest way to change a model's behavior.

1.title: Use Cases for Generative AI
1.text: Generative A I has many use cases. Image, video and audio generation: draft marketing images for a new destination. Summarization: short summaries of long guest reviews. A I assistants: a trip-planning helper. Translation: listings in many languages. Code generation: helping engineers write code. Customer service agents: handling booking changes. Search: finding policy answers by meaning. And recommendation engines: trip ideas written in a traveler's style. Exam tip: generating, summarizing or translating content is a generative A I use case.

1.title: The Foundation Model Lifecycle
1.text: The foundation model lifecycle has seven steps. The figure shows them. Data selection: choose and prepare broad data. Model selection: pick the base model that fits. Pre-training: train on huge data; builders do this, not most users. Fine-tuning: adapt the model to your task or domain. Then evaluation, deployment and feedback, and then improve and repeat. Exam tip: pre-training comes first and is huge, and fine-tuning comes after and is smaller.

1.title: Token-Based Pricing
1.text: Now cost. On Amazon Bedrock, on-demand pricing is per token: one price for input tokens and one for output tokens. Longer prompts and longer answers cost more, and they take longer. Batch inference is discounted for some models, by about fifty percent. Provisioned Throughput buys capacity per model unit for a commitment term, and it suits steady, high volume. Custom models add training, storage and inference charges. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, the details are on the Amazon Bedrock pricing page. Exam tip: variable use means pay per token, and steady, heavy use means consider provisioned throughput.

1.title: Context Engineering
1.text: A model sees only what is in its context window, and it keeps no memory by itself. Context engineering is deciding what goes into that window: instructions, retrieved documents, conversation history, memory and tool results. Better context gives better answers, and too much context raises cost and latency. Agents add short-term memory for a session, and long-term memory across sessions. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, A W S has no single definition page for this term, so this is the practice as its posts and documentation describe it. Exam tip: the right information, in the right amount, at the right time, is context engineering.

2.title: Agentic AI: Core Ideas
2.text: An A I agent uses a foundation model to reason about a goal and act on it. Tool usage means the agent calls tools, such as search, databases and A P Is. Memory management means it keeps context within a session and across sessions. Workflow orchestration means it plans steps, runs them and adapts. A single agent handles one job. A multi-agent system splits a complex job among specialist agents. Exam tip: reasoning, tools, memory and orchestration are the building blocks of an agent.

2.title: Multi-Agent Patterns
2.text: There are four multi-agent patterns to know. In agents as tools, a supervisor agent hands sub-tasks to specialist agents, as if calling tools. In a workflow, there is a fixed sequence of steps, each run by an agent. In a graph, agents are nodes and the edges decide the path. In a swarm, agents hand off work to one another as it unfolds. Agents talk to each other through communication patterns and open protocols, such as A two A, which stands for agent to agent. Exam tip: one coordinator with specialists means agents as tools, and fixed steps mean a workflow.

2.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
2.text: The Model Context Protocol, or M C P, is an open standard for connecting A I agents and models to external tools and data. It is often compared to a U S B C for A I applications: one standard plug. An M C P server exposes tools, resources and prompts, and an M C P client in the agent connects to it. AgentCore Gateway can turn A P Is and Lambda functions into M C P tools. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, see the A W S Prescriptive Guidance pages on agentic protocols. Exam tip: the role of M C P is one standard way to connect agents to external systems.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: GenAI Core Concepts
2.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Which term: token, chunk, embedding, vector, F M, L L M, transformer, multi-modal or diffusion. Which use case: generate, summarize, assist, translate, code, serve or search. Which lifecycle step: pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation or deployment. Which cost driver: input and output tokens, batch, or provisioned throughput. And which agent idea: tools, memory, orchestration, a multi-agent pattern, or M C P. Exam tip: name the idea in plain words first, then match it to the term.

2.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's GenAI Vocabulary
2.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and name the concept. Find review passages similar in meaning to a question: embeddings in a vector index. Split long policy P D Fs into pieces before indexing: chunking. Predict the bill for a month of chats: input and output tokens. Let a supervisor hand work to a flights agent and a hotels agent: multi-agent, with agents as tools. Let agents call external tools the same way: M C P. And order the lifecycle: data, model, pre-train, fine-tune, evaluate, deploy, feedback. Pause the video if you want more time.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Models: foundation models and L L Ms, transformers, multi-modal and diffusion models. Data in models: tokens, chunks, embeddings and vectors. Use cases: generate, summarize, assist, translate, code, serve, search and recommend. The lifecycle: data selection, model selection, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment and feedback. Cost: per input and output token, with batch and provisioned options. And agents: tools, memory, orchestration, multi-agent patterns and M C P.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which statement best describes a foundation model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: a large model pre-trained on broad, unlabeled data that can be adapted to many tasks. One model can handle many tasks when prompted or adapted. A single-task model, a rule engine and a vector database are different things.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Cedar and Salt wants to find guest-review passages that are close in meaning to a traveler's question, even when they share no exact words. What makes this possible? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, embeddings stored as vectors, compared by closeness of meaning. Embeddings put similar meanings close together, so a question can be matched to passages by meaning. Word counts, translation and sorting do not capture meaning.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two things affect the cost of a call to a foundation model that is billed per token? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. On-demand token pricing charges for input tokens, which come from the prompt, and for output tokens, which come from the response. Presentation choices and the number of readers do not change the token count.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Which kind of model generates an image by learning to remove noise step by step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, a diffusion model. Diffusion models are trained by adding noise to images and learning to reverse the process, so they can create a clear image from noise, often steered by a text prompt.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Which sequence lists the foundation model lifecycle in the correct order? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: data selection, model selection, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment and feedback. The lifecycle runs from data and model selection, through pre-training and fine-tuning, to evaluation, deployment and feedback, which leads back to earlier steps.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. What is the role of the Model Context Protocol, M C P, in agentic applications? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: it is an open standard for connecting agents to external tools and data. M C P lets agents and models reach tools, resources and data in a uniform way. It is not a training method, a compression method or a vector store.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Cedar and Salt builds a trip-planning system in which a supervisor agent hands flight searches to one specialist agent and hotel searches to another, then combines their results. Which pattern is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, a multi-agent system using agents as tools. A supervisor that delegates sub-tasks to specialist agents and merges their answers is a multi-agent pattern. A single agent with no tools, a batch job and a diffusion model do not describe it.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: B. Question two: D. Question three: A and C. Question four: A. Question five: C. Question six: B. Question seven: C. That completes Module four. Next, Module five looks at what generative A I does well, where it falls short, and how to judge whether a model delivers business value.
